# How Garmin inReach initiated my fiancée’s rescue


November 18, 2026


By Garmin team


### *When you’re deep in the backcountry, cellular coverage is spotty and you can’t count on it to raise the alarm in an emergency. Joe Keiser realized this when his fiancée, Marcela, badly injured her leg and needed a satellite-equipped device to summon search and rescue for evacuation. He shared the story with Garmin **.***


My fiancée of 20+ years, Marcela, lay helpless on the mountainside with her leg bent at a horrifying 45-degree angle just above the ankle. The joint itself pointed another 45 degrees in the opposite direction. It was the kind of injury you never forget, the kind that instantly turns a fun adventure into a nightmare.


We were deep in Idaho’s Sawtooth Wilderness near Smoky Dome, a brutal, remote stretch of wilderness where burned-over terrain has created miles of open isolation. We were 2 days from our car, miles from any recognizable trail, completely out of cell service and 4 miles away from our tent on a day hike. We hadn’t seen another human being in more than 3 days.


If I had left to get help, Marcela would likely have been alone for at least 24 hours.


## From peace of mind to necessity


A few months earlier, I had purchased a Garmin inReach®1 for one simple reason: my 90-year-old mother worried constantly whenever we disappeared into the backcountry.


After nearly 5 decades of backpacking Idaho wilderness areas with minimal issues, I figured the device was more for her peace of mind than for our peace of mind. Marcela and I had always made it back on our own 2 feet — maybe bruised, exhausted, or limping a little, but always self-sufficient.


I never imagined that the tiny orange device would one day really help us out.


*Correspondence from our great first responders*


## Pressing the SOS button


When reality finally hit me — *this isn’t just a sprain; this is life-threatening* — I pressed the SOS button on my inReach device. I also messaged my mother and daughter.


Minutes later, a message from the Garmin Response team appeared on the inReach screen and set my mind at ease:


*This is Garmin Response. What is your emergency?*


The sense of relief was overwhelming. Soon, I realized that Garmin Response had shared my information with Elmore County Dispatch, enabling two-way communication between us.


## A storm, a mountainside and no shelter


It was already 6:00 p.m. Dark storm clouds rolled toward us while we sat stranded on a 60-degree incline at 7,000 feet with no shelter and no idea when rescuers might arrive.


I wrapped Marcela’s ankle in crude figure-eights of duct tape, which were more symbolic first aid than anything useful. What she didn’t know was that her tibia was dangerously close to piercing through the skin. Her long pants and socks hid the worst of it, and I decided she didn’t need to hear that detail.


About a quarter of a mile downhill, there was a creek and a rare visible stretch of trail that hadn’t been swallowed by overgrowth. We decided that if we could somehow reach it, at least we’d have water and flatter ground to wait on.


Against all logic, I tried carrying Marcela. I took exactly one step before I slipped and collapsed. That was the moment I realized that I was not the mountain pack mule I imagined myself to be.


## Sliding down the mountain


Somehow, Marcela got herself downhill. Using the steep slope to her advantage, she lifted her shattered leg and slid herself down the mountainside through dirt, rocks and brush. By the time she reached the bottom, her pants were shredded and the pain had to be unimaginable.


Then another message arrived. Search and rescue had aborted the helicopter mission.


A storm was moving in, darkness was coming fast and fire activity in the area made flying too dangerous.


The next update said that a ground crew was preparing to hike in on foot. While we appreciated the effort, reality quickly set in. We were more than 20 miles from the trailhead in terrain that was difficult even with two healthy legs.


Eventually, that rescue plan was canceled too.


Another message from Garmin Response came shortly afterwardtolet us know that a helicopter would try again in the morning.Morning suddenly felt very far away.


## The longest night of our lives


As darkness settled over the mountains, the rain began.


About 20 yards away stood a large, burned pine tree that could have offered some shelter, but moving Marcela again risked forcing the bone through her skin. So we stayed where we were.


*Where we sat for 15 hours; ribbon put out to help the helicopter see us*


The temperature kept dropping.


Marcela put on a long-sleeve shirt she had packed. Beyond that, all we had to protect her from the storm was a backpack, my body heat, and — unexpectedly — a waterproof trail map.


That map — now framed and hanging prominently in our home — helped keep enough rain off her to avoid complete exposure. But at about 2:00 a.m., the hypothermic shivering began.


As the hours passed, Marcela’s skin turned paler, her breathing grew shallower and every hour felt heavier than the last.


The only thing keeping us mentally grounded was the steady stream of messages from the Garmin Response team and emergency responders and through the Garmin inReach screen. By then, my phone battery had died completely. It was just us, the rain and that tiny glowing screen in the wilderness.


## The helicopter arrives


The next morning, the rain finally eased.


Around 10:00 a.m., we heard the sound we’d been praying for: a helicopter.


The rescue crew was incredible. The captain descended from the hovering helicopter while the rotor blades whipped just feet from the mountainside. He initially reached for Tylenol, until he saw Marcela’s leg bent in two directions.


Then he immediately upgraded to a syringe with a stronger painkiller.


The captain asked me to hold Marcela’s leg while he splinted it. My gut instinct said, “No,” but I grabbed hold and looked away while he worked.


## The walk back alone


*Marcela landing at the base before being rushed to the hospital*


Marcela was flown to the hospital suffering from hypothermia, dehydration (turns out, drinking water isn’t top of mind when your leg is in pieces and you’re shivering) and a dangerously weak heartbeat. Doctors treated these issues before even beginning to repair her broken leg.


Meanwhile, I hiked back to our tent alone, packed our gear and spent the next 26 hours hiking back to our car.


In all that time, I never saw a single person on the trail or even in the parking lot, which showed just how isolated we were. A week later, Marcela underwent surgery to repair her fractured tibia and ankle. Metal pins, scars on both sides of her leg and months of recovery followed.


Today? She’s 100% healed and ready for our future exploring.


## The next adventure


*Happy times in between dire strait times*


Two years later, we finally did it. After more than 20 years together — and one dramatic reminder that life doesn’t always follow the itinerary — Marcela and I tied the knot beside one of our favorite alpine lakes.


Naturally, we chose one of the most remote lakes in the Sawtooth Wilderness. Apparently, one helicopter rescue wasn’t enough to convince us that a courthouse might be easier! This time, the emergency plan was replaced with a wedding itinerary. It was just the 2 of us at the lake, while our family, friends and marriage minister joined us by Zoom.


A mini Starlink handled the connection, and our trusty Garmin inReach came along for last-minute planning and invitations. Two years earlier, those satellite messages were helping coordinate a rescue through the Garmin Response team. This time, they were helping coordinate a wedding. That felt like a pretty good upgrade.


No shattered leg. No hypothermia. No rescue helicopter. Just the Sawtooths, a Zoom call and finally saying “I do.”
